Do we consider DF a roguelike around these here parts?

As much as many people hate it, I find that the Berlin Interpretation is a good way to judge roguelike-ness.

DF hits most of the high value targets.

Random environment generation

Check

Permadeath

Check

Turn-based

Check

Grid-based

Check

Non-modal

Not check, it does have an overworld.

Complexity

I feel like it deserves two check marks.

Resource management

Check

Hack'n'slash

Lots of combat, check here

Exploration and discovery

No unidentified items in exploration mode, so half a checkmark here.

Total, 7-8 out of 9. Most people consider anything 6 or above to be a "Roguelike" via the modern definition. Binding of Isaac is a 6. FTL is 6. ADoM and Crawl are only 8s on the above list.
I've never seen the Berlin Interpretation before, that's interesting! TIL, thank you!
Be warned that a lot of people really strongly dislike it. But I've yet to see a solid argument for why it's a bad definition to use when defining what is a roguelike and what is not.

I'd say the problem with the Berlin interpretation is that it's too restrictive for many folks tastes. On the other hand though, I'd say that Binding of Isaac and FTL are clearly NOT roguelikes. Different features have different amounts of weight when it comes to determining a roguelike. For instance, if it's not turn based, it's not a roguelike, end of discussion, whereas non-modal is far less important. Even DCSS has a shop screen.

I'd assign several tiers of importance to the factors listed as part of the BI, which don't agree with it fully.

Tier 1: Turn based, permadeath, complexity, and procedural levels, Tactical challenge (Even in relatively non-spoiler needing games like DCSS, knowing what you're fighting and how the mechanics work is how you win)

Tier 2: Hack and Slash, Gridbased (Do all mobs REALLY need to take up only one tile? OFC not) , Exploration (take DCSS, if you spriggan dive you don't explore much at all. Cogmind also discourages over-exploration), Single Player Character (this is not essential, but it's pretty important), Same rules for players and monsters, numbers

Tier 3: ASCII (ascii hasn't mattered to the genre for decades now), Dungeons (dungeons certainly help, but other environments work just as well. Wayward is a fine exqmple with the deserted island theme)

Tier fuck the BI: non-modal. The single screen shit is silly. Even DCSS has other screen and interfaces, especially in webtiles.

EDIT: as for the matter of Dorf Fortress, adventure mode at least is pretty clearly a roguelike by my definitions, even without meeting a strict turnbased requirement. Fortress mode is another story. It does match many of the standards, but it very flagrantly does not match the single player aspect. It does so in a way where you don't even identify with specific characters at all, because you're more of a dungeon keeper style overlord. I'd call it a roguelite, but the term "lite" really isn't appropriate for anything Dorf related, and FTL, Spelunky, or BoI are more fitting for that term.

For instance, if it's not turn based, it's not a roguelike, end of discussion

MAngband. It's 100% roguelike, but it is realtime (in that the game processes chunks of actions every X seconds, for necessity). There are plenty of other examples out there of clearly roguelike games with realtime execution.

You've also made a very confusing argument. Berlin can't be both "too restrictive" and then "not restrictive enough". The above argument is taking both sides of the discussion. Both claiming that Berlin is too restrictive, and then coming up with rules that are vastly more restrictive.

The problem with your definition is that it is too wishy washy. There are a lot of subjective calls that are hard to pin down. That's now how you want to define a game or a genre. You want concrete rules that can be applied to make it clear what does and does not fit.
Hmm, I'd say the main game belongs in the "monster management" category, akin to dungeon keeper, but the adventurer mode is definitely a roguelike.

I feel a bit bad necroing this post, but it looks like this sub is a bit slow anyway... I think DF is a roguelike for sure. Even if you don't consider fortress mode strictly roguelike, the game still has adventure mode, which by any definition is a roguelike.

The current one-vote voting system in Straw Poll can be ineffective and give less-than-desirable results. For example, if two options are very similar, they would lose votes to each other even though they would win if combined together. The final winner could win with just a small fraction of the total votes, and with all the other voters hating the final result. An easy solution to this is to implement Approval Voting. Voters get to approve or disapprove each and every option. The option that satisfies the most voters wins. Here is a CGP Grey video on it.
